blurb: Point-source capture, direct air capture, ocean and mineral removal, biomass and land sinks, plus the pipelines and pore space that store the CO2 — with cost per ton, permanence, and how much of each is actually running.
question: How does this CO2 get captured, and what does a ton cost?
title: Carbon Capture and Removal: A Practical Reference
lede: Two different businesses get talked about as one. Point-source capture keeps CO2 out of the air and competes against the cost of emitting it; removal takes CO2 back out and competes against other removals on price and permanence. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} approaches across seven classes, with cost per ton, storage permanence, and how much of each is operating rather than announced.

groupBlurbs.Sorbents & membranes: solids and films that skip the boiling step
groupBlurbs.Pre-combustion & oxy-fuel: capture before combustion, or burn without nitrogen
groupBlurbs.Looping & process streams: circulating carriers, and the CO2 that arrives pure

facets.label: Feed
facets.tip: Where the CO2 comes from. Flue gas is 3–15% CO2 and sets the cost of most point-source capture · Process stream is 90%+ and is the cheapest CO2 anywhere · Ambient air is 0.042% · Biogenic means the carbon came from recent photosynthesis · Any source covers transport, storage, and utilization, which take CO2 from whatever produced it.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional all-in cost per net ton of CO2 captured, removed, or handled, at the scale the approach runs today. Removal numbers are what a buyer pays; capture numbers are the levelized cost on the plant. Early-stage approaches are tagged at today's cost, not at their target.

facets.label: Permanence
facets.tip: How long the carbon stays put once the approach has done its job, and how reversible that is. Untagged on capture technologies, whose permanence is decided by the storage they feed rather than by the capture step.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Commercial = multiple plants running on commercial terms · First-of-a-kind = one or two full-scale units built or building · Pilot = demonstration hardware in the field · Lab = bench and modeling only.

facets.label: Deployed
facets.tip: Roughly how much CO2 the approach actually handles worldwide today, per year. This is the field that separates a 1 Mt/yr industry from a 1,000 t/yr pilot, and it is the number press releases most often skip.
